Title: Vehicle-to-grid power fundamentals: Calculating capacity and net revenue
Abstract: As the light vehicle fleet moves to electric drive (hybrid, battery, and fuel cell vehicles), an opportunity opens for “vehicle-to-grid” (V2G) power. This article defines the three vehicle types that can produce V2G power, and the power markets they can sell into. V2G only makes sense if the vehicle and power market are matched. For example, V2G appears to be unsuitable for baseload power—the constant round-the-clock electricity supply—because baseload power can be provided more cheaply by large generators, as it is today. Rather, V2G's greatest near-term promise is for quick-response, high-value electric services. These quick-response electric services are purchased to balance constant fluctuations in load and to adapt to unexpected equipment failures; they account for 5–10% of electric cost—$ 12 billion per year in the US. This article develops equations to calculate the capacity for grid power from three types of electric drive vehicles. These equations are applied to evaluate revenue and costs for these vehicles to supply electricity to three electric markets (peak power, spinning reserves, and regulation). The results suggest that the engineering rationale and economic motivation for V2G power are compelling. The societal advantages of developing V2G include an additional revenue stream for cleaner vehicles, increased stability and reliability of the electric grid, lower electric system costs, and eventually, inexpensive storage and backup for renewable electricity.

Title: Is awareness of public charging associated with consumer interest in plug-in electric vehicles?
Abstract: Policymakers often seek to increase the visibility of plug-in electric vehicle (PEV) chargers in public locations in effort to build familiarity and interest in PEVs. However, it is not clear if the visibility of public charging stations actually has an impact on PEV demand. The purposes of the present study are to (1) assess the current levels of visibility for public PEV charging infrastructure within Canada and (2) identify whether or not a statistically significant relationship exists between consumer awareness of public charging infrastructure and interest in purchasing a PEV. We use data collected from a sample of 1739 Canadian new-vehicle buyers in 2013. About 18% of Canadian respondents have seen at least one public charger, while the proportion is highest in British Columbia (31%). We find a significant bivariate relationship between public charger awareness and PEV interest. However, when controlling for multiple explanatory variables in regression analyses, the relationship is weak or non-existent. While perceived existence of at least one charger exhibits no significant relationship with PEV interest, perceived existence of multiple chargers can have a weak but significant relationship. Thus, public charger awareness is not a strong predictor of PEV interest; other variables are more important, such as the availability of level 1 (110/120-volt) charging at home.

gold.abstract: This paper investigates the economic impact of vehicle-home-grid integration, by proposing an online energy management algorithm that optimizes energy flows between an electric vehicle (EV), a household, and the electrical grid. The algorithm leverages vehicle-to-home (V2H) for self-consumption and vehicle-to-grid (V2G) for energy trading, adapting to real-time conditions through a hybrid long short-term memory (LSTM) neural network for accurate household load prediction, alongside a comprehensive nonlinear battery degradation model accounting for both cycle and calendar aging. Simulation results reveal significant economic advantages: compared to smart unidirectional charging, the proposed method yields an annual economic benefit of up to EUR 3046.81, despite a modest 1.96% increase in battery degradation. Even under unfavorable market conditions, where V2G energy selling generates no revenue, V2H alone ensures yearly savings of EUR 425.48. A systematic sensitivity analysis investigates how variations in battery capacity, household load, and price ratios affect economic outcomes, confirming the consistent benefits of bidirectional energy exchange. These findings highlight the potential of EVs as active energy nodes, enabling sustainable energy management and cost-effective battery usage in real-world conditions.

These are your colleagues' latest proposals:

--- Researcher B ---
SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
- Paper-b contributes engineering-economic equations that calculate vehicle-to-grid (V2G) capacity and net revenue for electric-drive vehicles in peak power, spinning reserves, and regulation markets. It shows V2G is best suited to high-value quick-response services, not baseload.

Awareness alone does not make public charging valuable to consumers (paper-c). But paper-b’s revenue equations can convert a consumer’s vehicle use and local market conditions into a personalized V2G revenue estimate. The proposed mechanism is that combining public charger awareness with a concrete V2G revenue calculation changes the economic meaning of that infrastructure, potentially strengthening PEV interest. Run a survey experiment with new-vehicle buyers. Measure baseline PEV interest, home charging access, public charger awareness (none/single/multiple), driving patterns, and location. Randomize respondents to either generic PEV information or generic information plus a personalized V2G revenue estimate calculated using paper-b’s equations for peak, spinning reserve, and regulation markets. Validate revenue estimates against local market prices. Use regression controlling for paper-c’s variables, testing the interaction between treatment and charger awareness. Outcome: PEV interest and stated willingness to enroll in V2G.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
This study tests whether adding a personalized V2G revenue estimate to public charging information increases PEV interest more than awareness alone. It links engineering-based V2G capacity and revenue calculations from paper-b to consumer charger-awareness findings from paper-c, addressing whether economic value can activate infrastructure awareness.

FINAL IDEA: Personalized V2G revenue calculations derived from vehicle-to-grid capacity equations may convert weak public charger awareness into stronger plug-in electric vehicle interest by making charging infrastructure economically meaningful to consumers.

--- Researcher C ---
SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
- Paper B: Provides equations for V2G capacity and net revenue for electric drive vehicles across peak power, spinning reserves, and regulation markets; finds V2G economically compelling for high-value, quick-response grid services.
- Paper C: Survey of 1,739 Canadian new-vehicle buyers shows public charger awareness is a weak or non-significant predictor of PEV interest after controls; home Level 1 charging availability is a stronger predictor.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
V2G revenue is operationally conditional on a dedicated home charging connection with bidirectional capability and predictable plug-in schedules, not on public charger visibility. Paper C identifies home charging as the salient adoption factor; Paper B supplies the economic magnitude of that home connection’s V2G value. The causal link is: perceived V2G net revenue, calculated via Paper B’s equations, should interact with home charging availability to increase PEV interest, while public charger awareness remains non-causal.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
Randomized 2×2 survey experiment on Canadian new-vehicle buyers (replicating Paper C sampling). Factor 1: personalized V2G revenue treatment using Paper B’s equations (battery size, daily driving, local regulation/spinning reserve prices) versus generic environmental information. Factor 2: home charging availability prompt/actual status. Outcomes: PEV purchase interest, willingness to pay for bidirectional charger, perceived V2G revenue. Controls from Paper C: home Level 1 charging, charger awareness, demographics. Analyze treatment×home charging interaction; expect V2G effect only among home-charging-capable respondents. Validate by comparing calculated V2G revenue with self-reported estimates and six-month follow-up on actual PEV purchase or bidirectional charger installation.
Missing cross-paper knowledge: neither source measures V2G revenue expectations, bidirectional charging capability, or the home-charging/V2G interaction; no longitudinal behavioral data.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
This project tests whether V2G revenue potential converts home charging access into PEV demand. Paper B supplies equations to calculate individualized V2G capacity and net revenue for high-value grid services; Paper C shows home charging, not public charger awareness, predicts PEV interest. We propose a randomized survey experiment providing personalized V2G revenue estimates to home-charging-capable and non-capable buyers. We expect V2G framing to increase interest primarily among those with home charging, clarifying a demand-side mechanism for V2G adoption and informing targeted incentive design.

FINAL IDEA: Test whether personalized V2G revenue estimates calculated from vehicle-to-grid capacity equations increase plug-in electric vehicle purchase interest primarily among households with home charging access, as implied by Paper C’s finding that public charger awareness does not.
